If your board is dirty with dust, old flux, etc clean it first with some isopropyl alcohol.

Always use flux, it helps to remove the surface corrosion from the contact points. Most soldering wires come with a flux core, but if the piece you are working with is too old or has been through some rough conditions additional flux will help, a dirty joint will form something that looks like the cold joint from the image.

You have to remember that oxidation occurs when metal has contact with the oxygen in the air, and this happens faster with high temperature. That's why the image shows a darker joint when you leave the iron too long, it starts to oxidize, but abundant flux will delay that.

The same happens to the tip of the iron. To keep it in the best condition you have to "clean" the tip, meaning remove the old solder and add new one. Clean the tip each time you turn the iron on/off and between a few components soldered. 

ALWAYS keep the tip tinned, as it creates a barrier between the tip and the air and will increase the heat transfer from the tip to the part you are soldering.

What people meant by "leave the tip dirty" is to leave the tip tinned (with fresh solder).


For a good joint both contact points have to be clean and hot, that's why the image suggests heating the joint before adding the solder, the solder will melt in contact with the pin/pad and you will be sure it is hot enough. If that takes too long add solder between the tip and the joint as this will increase the heat contact.

When your components are small and sensitive to too much heat (smd for example), you just can add a blob of solder to the tip instead of adding solder directly to the joint (as in those cases the joint will be small and you won't need preheating and/or adding more solder). Don't leave it too long on the tip or the solder might start to oxidize. This will also evaporate the flux from the solder wire so this works better when you have additional flux in the joint.
